prize_parts.citation: For discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and its development into long-acting incretin therapies for diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: All six of us placed GLP-1 first, and the agreement rests on the science, not on momentum. The arc runs from hormone physiology (Holst's work on GLP-1 secretion and action in humans, Drucker's proglucagon and intestinotrophic biology) through to long-acting acylated analogues (Knudsen) that are now used at very large scale. It is a specific discovery that has changed a field. The change is visible in how type 2 diabetes and obesity are treated, and increasingly in cardiovascular and renal outcomes. Efficacy has been confirmed by several large independent outcome trials, so there is no maturity concern. I keep the Drucker, Holst and Knudsen trio because it covers both the physiological discovery and the translation that made it a medicine, and it is the configuration four of six of us proposed in the opening round.
statement.case_against: The attribution problem is real and I do not think the committee should wave it away. Svetlana Mojsov's identification and synthesis of the active GLP-1 peptide forms is a credible claim, and priority around early GLP-1 work (including Habener, who is not on the credited list) is contested. Any three-person limit leaves out at least one well-credited person. A discovery-only prize would look different from a discovery-plus-drug prize. Placing a drug developer next to the physiologists could also be read as favouring industrial development over discovery.

responses.point: Per ranks GLP-1 first but credits Mojsov in place of Knudsen, because Mojsov identified the active peptide form and the discovery chain is what the prize should reward. He also wants the prize to cover the gut-brain hormone concept.
responses.response: I take the point about Mojsov seriously, and a prize framed around the discovery of the active peptide would make the case for her stronger. I still prefer Knudsen. Without the acylated analogues, GLP-1 biology would not have become a therapy, and the clinical effect is the reason this prize is timely. The active form had also been characterised independently by Holst and others, so I find Mojsov's discovery claim less separable from the physiology than Per does. I regard this as a judgement call and not a clear error on either side. I would revisit it if the committee frames the citation around discovery only.

responses.point: Marie credits Holst, Drucker and Mojsov and treats Knudsen's medicinal chemistry as major but closer to drug development. She also notes that priority disputes around early GLP-1 work remain.
responses.response: The priority disputes are the strongest argument for being cautious about naming the peptide-identification step. That is also why I would anchor the citation in physiology and therapeutic development, where the lines of credit are clearer. I do not agree that drug design is a lesser category here. Long-acting analogues required real conceptual work on half-life and albumin binding, and past Physiology or Medicine prizes have recognised translation when a discovery gave a new therapeutic principle. I do share her view that this needs to be settled explicitly and not by default.

responses.point: Abdel places optogenetics second and cGAS-STING fourth, proposing Chen alone for cGAS-STING. His view is that optogenetics is a causal method that reshaped circuit analysis, with clinical use still emerging.
responses.response: I agree that optogenetics changed neuroscience, and it is my third choice. My reservation is that it is mainly a research tool and that six credited names compete for three places, so any trio will be contested. I rank CAR-T above it because CAR-T has a demonstrated patient benefit and a more compact credit structure. Abdel's Chen-alone proposal for cGAS-STING is defensible on the evidence for cGAS and cGAMP, but I would pair Chen with Barber for STING if that candidate came forward, and I think therapeutic translation is too immature to treat it as a competitor this year.

responses.point: Sten places CAR-T second and the SMN2 antisense work third, calling the Krainer and Bennett credit clean and the rationale well supported by approval since 2016.
responses.response: The two-person credit for nusinersen is cleaner than that for any other candidate except the unfolded protein response. It has also converted a fatal infantile disease into a treatable one, which I take as a strong argument. I did not rank it in my top eight, and I stand by that, because the case rests on one drug and long-term durability against gene therapy is still being established. I would be willing to see it as a later prize, but I do not see it competing with GLP-1 now.

uncertainties: How to allocate the three places among Drucker, Holst, Knudsen and Mojsov, and whether the citation should centre on discovery or on discovery plus drug development.
Whether the contested priority claims on early GLP-1 work (Mojsov, Habener and others) can be resolved from the supplied evidence.
If GLP-1 is awarded, whether CAR-T or optogenetics is the better candidate for a future prize, which depends on how the committee weighs a clinical therapy against a research method.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile for the GLP-1, CAR-T or optogenetics candidates. My documented ties are to nuclear-receptor work with Ronald Evans, collaboration with Johan Ericson, and co-authorship with Per Svenningsson and Abdel El Manira, none of which concerns the shortlisted candidates.
